MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. arXiv:2311.16502.
creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen (IN.AI Research, University of Waterloo, The Ohio State University, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Victoria, Princeton University)
description: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning) is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines (Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering) across 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.
name: MMMU
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question was annotated with question type, question text, answer options (for multiple-choice), correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation (if available). A secondary review team additionally vetted each annotation for quality.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in the 30 covered subjects, recruited from multiple universities. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent experts across the 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A secondary review team vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Regular audits of random samples were conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency. Ambiguities were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings. Human expert performance on the validation set ranged from 76.2% (worst) to 88.6% (best), with a median of 82.6%, establishing the human performance ceiling.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom web interface developed for data annotation and verification (developed by Tianyu Zheng)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators collected multimodal questions from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, and other study materials. Questions must contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and not be ambiguous. Each question was annotated with: question type (multiple-choice or open-ended), question text, answer options (for multiple-choice), correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation (if available). Data was stored in JSON format. Annotators were instructed to avoid copyright-restricted sources and to select questions whose answers are not immediately accessible. Questions were categorized into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard); approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded.
rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases (explicitly acknowledged by the authors). Annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers to mitigate data contamination concerns with foundation models. Questions were selected to avoid those from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. The benchmark focuses on college-level subjects, which may not represent all aspects of expert knowledge.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected in three stages. First, 30 subjects from six disciplines were selected based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted. Second, over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in these majors were recruited as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks, online resources, and lecture materials, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to select questions without immediately available answers (e.g., answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks). This process resulted in a diverse collection of approximately 13K questions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions collected from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, online resources, and lecture materials across 30 subjects and 6 disciplines. The raw collection comprised approximately 13K questions before quality filtering.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI as defined by Morris et al. There is no direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The benchmark is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI. Some subjects like law and linguistics were excluded because it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two-stage data cleaning: (1) Lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications. (2) Problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking, ensuring adherence to a standardized format. (3) Problems were categorized into four difficulty levels; approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU is intended to stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence. The benchmark relates to monitoring progress towards Expert AGI (Level 3 in Morris et al.'s taxonomy), which denotes AI reaching "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks, with potential for significant job displacement and economic disruption. The authors caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI but should be a necessary criterion for any Expert AGI system.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal foundation models on college-level multi-discipline understanding and reasoning tasks; benchmarking progress towards Expert AGI; assessing expert-level visual perception, domain knowledge recall, and deliberate reasoning capabilities of large multimodal models (LMMs); identifying model weaknesses in perceptual errors, knowledge gaps, and reasoning failures across diverse academic disciplines.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotators were instructed to avoid collecting questions that contain any private information, in compliance with privacy laws and ethical standards in data handling.
